title: Catalan grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is central Catalan, as it is spoken in Barcelona, in the current spelling.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Catalan conversation.
lessons.topic: {{em dic}} and {{et dius}}; {{soc}}, {{ets}}, {{és}} “I am, you are, he or she is”; {{de}} “from”

goal.t: Hola, em dic Laura. Soc de Boston.
goal.tr: Hi, my name's Laura. I'm from Boston.

dialog.t: Hola! Em dic Marc.
dialog.tr: Hi! My name's Marc.

dialog.t: Hola, Marc. Jo em dic Laura.
dialog.tr: Hi, Marc. I'm Laura.

dialog.t: D'on ets?
dialog.tr: Where are you from?

dialog.t: Soc de Boston. I tu?
dialog.tr: I'm from Boston. And you?

dialog.t: Jo soc d'aquí, de Barcelona. Encantat!
dialog.tr: I'm from here, from Barcelona. Nice to meet you!

dialog.t: Encantada!
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: **Saying your name.** Catalans say {{em dic}}, word for word “I call myself”: {{Em dic Laura.}} “My name's Laura.” To ask, {{Com et dius?}} “What's your name?”, word for word “how do you call yourself?”. The little words {{em}} “myself” and {{et}} “yourself” go before the verb. You'll meet many more little words like them: they are one of the things that make Catalan Catalan.

blocks.means: a word for doing or being: go, eat, live, call, be.

blocks.p: **I'm, you're.** “To be” is {{ser}}: {{soc}} “I am”, {{ets}} “you are”, {{és}} “he is, she is”. There is no word for “I” in {{Soc de Boston}}: the verb's ending already says who it is, so Catalan usually leaves “I” and “you” out. You add {{jo}} “I” or {{tu}} “you” only for a contrast: {{Jo soc d'aquí.}} “I'm from here (and you aren't).”

table: {{Ets de Barcelona?}} Are you from Barcelona?

blocks.p: **Where from.** {{de}} is “from” (and “of”). Before a vowel it becomes {{d'}}: {{D'on ets?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “from where are you?”. The “from” always goes first, never at the end. {{I tu?}} “And you?” turns any question back to the other person.

ex.note: many cities have a Catalan name: {{Londres}}, {{Nova York}}
a question just by raising your voice at the end
{{és}} is both “he is” and “she is”: the conversation tells you who
the same for a man or a woman

blocks.tip: {{Encantat}} is said by a man, {{encantada}} by a woman: Catalan words often take an {{-a}} for a woman (lesson 3). Greetings: {{Bon dia}} “good morning” (until lunch), {{Bona tarda}} “good afternoon, good evening”, {{Bona nit}} “good night”, {{Adeu}} “bye”, {{Fins després}} “see you later”.

mistakes.why: “From” goes in front of “where”, never at the end: {{d'on}}.
{{de}} becomes {{d'}} before a vowel.

lessons.title: Order in a café
lessons.summary: Ask for what you'd like in a café or a shop, politely: “I'd like a coffee with milk, please.”
lessons.topic: {{vull}} and {{voldria}} + a thing; {{un}} and {{una}} “a”; no word for “some”; {{no}}

goal.t: Voldria un cafè amb llet, si us plau.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

dialog.t: Bon dia! Què et poso?
dialog.tr: Good morning! What can I get you?

dialog.t: Bon dia. Voldria un cafè amb llet, si us plau.
dialog.tr: Good morning. I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

dialog.t: Alguna cosa més?
dialog.tr: Anything else?

dialog.t: Sí, un croissant. I una aigua.
dialog.tr: Yes, a croissant. And a water.

dialog.t: Amb gas o sense?
dialog.tr: Sparkling or still?

dialog.t: Sense gas. Gràcies!
dialog.tr: Still. Thanks!

blocks.p: **Asking for something.** {{Voldria}} “I'd like” is the polite way, good anywhere. {{Vull}} “I want” is fine too, with {{si us plau}} “please”: {{Vull un tallat, si us plau.}} “A cortado, please.” Then say thanks: {{gràcies}}, or {{moltes gràcies}} “thank you very much”.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: coffee, waiter, Barcelona.

blocks.p: **A, an.** Catalan has two words for “a”: {{un}} and {{una}}. Every noun is either masculine or feminine (lesson 4 explains), and “a” matches it: {{un cafè}} “a coffee”, but {{una aigua}} “a water”, {{una cervesa}} “a beer”. Nouns ending in {{-a}} nearly always take {{una}}; learn the others with their {{un}} or {{una}}.

table: {{un suc de taronja}} an orange juice
{{una ampolla de vi}} a bottle of wine

blocks.p: **No word for “some”.** For things you don't count, like bread, milk or water, Catalan uses the noun alone: {{Vull pa.}} “I'd like some bread.” {{Tens llet?}} “Do you have any milk?”.
**Not.** {{no}} goes right before the verb: {{No vull sucre.}} “I don't want sugar.”

ex.tr: I'd like a ham sandwich, please.
I'd like a bottle of water.

ex.tr: A cortado and a croissant, please.

{{vols}} “you want”

lessons.title: Say who people are and what they're like
lessons.summary: Introduce your friends and describe people: “Jordi and I are friends. He's from Girona, and he's very nice.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} “to be” for everyone; {{jo, tu, ell, ella…}}; adjectives for a man, a woman, and more than one; {{en}} and {{la}} before names

goal.t: En Jordi i jo som amics. És de Girona i és molt simpàtic.
goal.tr: Jordi and I are friends. He's from Girona, and he's very nice.

dialog.t: Qui és la noia de la foto?
dialog.tr: Who's the girl in the photo?

dialog.t: És la Clara. És de Tarragona.
dialog.tr: That's Clara. She's from Tarragona.

dialog.t: I com és?
dialog.tr: And what's she like?

dialog.t: És molt simpàtica i una mica tímida.
dialog.tr: She's very nice and a little shy.

dialog.t: I els dos nois?
dialog.tr: And the two guys?

dialog.t: Són en Pere i en Joan. Són bessons!
dialog.tr: They're Pere and Joan. They're twins!

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, she, they.

blocks.p: **The whole verb.** Here is {{ser}} “to be” for everyone. The ending tells you who it is, so the pronouns are usually left out; you say them for a contrast, or when it wouldn't be clear: {{Ell és de Girona, i ella és de Vic.}} “He's from Girona, and she's from Vic.”

**{{tu}} or {{vostè}}?** {{tu}} is for friends, family, children and people your age, and it's what Catalans use most. {{vostè}} is the polite “you”, for older people and formal moments, and it takes the verb of “he, she”: {{Vostè és de Lleida?}} “Are you from Lleida?”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: tall, nice, new.

blocks.p: **Describing a man or a woman.** Adjectives change to match the person. Most add {{-a}} for a woman: {{alt}} → {{alta}} “tall”, {{simpàtic}} → {{simpàtica}} “nice”. Many that end in {{-e}} stay the same: {{jove}} “young”, {{amable}} “kind”. For more than one, add {{-s}}, and for women change {{-a}} to {{-es}}: {{Són alts.}} “They're tall (men, or a mixed group).” {{Són altes.}} “They're tall (women).”

**Names take an article.** In everyday Catalan a name has a little word in front: {{en}} for a man, {{la}} for a woman, and {{l'}} for anyone whose name starts with a vowel: {{en Jordi}}, {{la Clara}}, {{l'Anna}}, {{l'Oriol}}. You leave it out when you speak to the person: {{Hola, Clara!}}

ex.t: En Pere i en Joan són alts.

ex.note: no word for “a” before a job
the polite {{vostè}}, with {{és}}

blocks.tip: {{jo}} “I” has a small letter, unlike English “I”. In Mallorca, and in some formal writing, you'll see {{na}} instead of {{la}} before a woman's name: {{na Maria}}.

mistakes.why: Clara is a woman: the adjective takes {{-a}}.
After {{ser}}, a job has no “a”: {{és professora}}.

lessons.title: Name things: “the”, “a” and more than one
lessons.summary: Name the things around you, one or many: “the keys”, “a table”, “two beers”.
lessons.topic: Masculine and feminine; {{el, la, l', els, les}} “the”; {{un, una, uns, unes}}; plurals; {{dos}}, {{dues}}

goal.t: Dos cafès i una aigua, si us plau.
goal.tr: Two coffees and a water, please.

blocks.means: whether a noun is masculine or feminine. In Catalan every noun has one, even things, and the words around it change to match.

blocks.p: **Masculine and feminine.** {{el llibre}} “the book” is masculine, {{la taula}} “the table” is feminine. There's no logic to it, but there's a strong hint: nouns ending in {{-a}} are nearly always feminine ({{la casa}} “the house”, {{la porta}} “the door”). A few aren't: {{el dia}} “the day” and {{el pa}} “the bread” are masculine. Nouns with other endings can be either: {{el cotxe}} “the car”, but {{la clau}} “the key”.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun: “the” or “a”.

blocks.p: **{{l'}}.** Before a vowel, or an {{h}} (always silent in Catalan), {{el}} and {{la}} both become {{l'}}: {{l'aigua}} “the water”, {{l'home}} “the man”. {{els}}, {{les}}, {{un}} and {{una}} never change.

blocks.means: the form of a word for more than one: books, tables. The form for one is the singular.

blocks.p: **More than one.** Most nouns add {{-s}}: {{el cotxe}} → {{els cotxes}}, {{el cafè}} → {{els cafès}}. A final {{-a}} becomes {{-es}}: {{la casa}} → {{les cases}}, {{la cervesa}} → {{les cerveses}}; sometimes the spelling shifts to keep the sound, as in {{amiga}} → {{amigues}}. Masculine nouns ending in {{-s}} add {{-os}}: {{el gos}} → {{els gossos}} “the dogs”. And nouns ending in a stressed vowel add {{-ns}}: {{l'entrepà}} → {{els entrepans}} “the sandwiches”.
**One and two.** “One” and “two” have a feminine: {{un cafè}}, {{una aigua}}; {{dos cafès}}, {{dues cerveses}}. From three on, numbers don't change: {{tres cafès}}, {{tres cerveses}}.

ex.note: {{pa}} ends in {{-a}} but is masculine

ex.t: Són uns amics de la Clara.

blocks.tip: Learn each noun with its article, {{el pa}}, {{la llet}} “the milk”, {{la nit}} “the night”: the article tells you its gender, and its gender changes the words around it.

mistakes.why: {{cervesa}} is feminine, so “two” is {{dues}}.
Before a vowel or a silent {{h}}, “the” is {{l'}}.
{{cotxe}} is masculine, so “the” in the plural is {{els}}.

practice.why: A final {{-a}} becomes {{-es}} in the plural: {{cerveses}}.
A masculine noun ending in {{-s}} adds {{-os}}: {{els gossos}}.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask who, what, where, when, how and why, and ask yes-or-no questions just with your voice.
lessons.topic: Question words: {{què, qui, on, quan, com, per què, quant, quin}}; questions by intonation; {{oi?}}

goal.t: On vius? I què fas?
goal.tr: Where do you live? And what do you do?

dialog.t: Hola! Com et dius?
dialog.tr: Hi! What's your name?

dialog.t: Ben. I tu?
dialog.tr: Ben. And you?

dialog.t: Marta. Ets anglès?
dialog.tr: Marta. Are you English?

dialog.t: No, soc irlandès, de Dublín.
dialog.tr: No, I'm Irish, from Dublin.

dialog.t: I què fas a Barcelona?
dialog.tr: And what are you doing in Barcelona?

dialog.t: Estudio a la universitat. I tu, on vius?
dialog.tr: I'm studying at the university. And you, where do you live?

dialog.t: A Gràcia, a prop d'aquí.
dialog.tr: In Gràcia, near here.

blocks.p: **Yes or no.** A yes-or-no question is the same sentence said with your voice going up: {{Ets anglès.}} “You're English.” → {{Ets anglès?}} “Are you English?”. Nothing moves, and there's no word like “do”: {{Parles català?}} “Do you speak Catalan?”. In speech you'll often hear {{que}} at the start, just to signal a question: {{Que ets anglès?}}. And {{oi?}} at the end means “right?”: {{Ets d'aquí, oi?}} “You're from here, right?”.

table: {{Per què estudies català?}} Why are you learning Catalan?
{{Quin dia és avui?}} What day is it today?

blocks.p: **The question word comes first**, then the verb, and the person (if you say who) after it: {{On viu la Marta?}} “Where does Marta live?”. A little word like “from” or “with” goes in front of the question word, never at the end: {{D'on ets?}} “Where are you from?”, {{Amb qui vius?}} “Who do you live with?”.
**Accents.** {{què}} “what” has an accent, which tells it apart from {{que}} “that”. “Why” is two words, {{per què}}, while the answer “because” is one: {{perquè}}.

ex.note: {{vens}} “you come”

blocks.tip: {{Com?}} on its own means “Sorry?”, when you didn't catch something. More polite: {{Perdona, pots repetir?}} “Sorry, can you say that again?”.

mistakes.why: A word like {{amb}} “with” goes in front of the question word, never at the end.
“What” is {{què}}, with an accent.

mistakes.wrong: Per què? Per què és tard.
mistakes.why: “Why” is {{per què}}, two words; “because” is {{perquè}}, one word.

lessons.title: Ask where things are
lessons.summary: Ask the way and say where things are: “Excuse me, where's the station? —It's next to the market.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} for where things are: {{On és…? És a…}}; {{al}}, {{del}}, {{pel}}; place words: {{a prop de, al costat de, davant de…}}

goal.t: Perdoni, on és l'estació?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the station?

dialog.t: Perdoni, on és l'estació de tren?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the train station?

dialog.t: És a prop, al final d'aquest carrer.
dialog.tr: It's close, at the end of this street.

dialog.t: I la farmàcia?
dialog.tr: And the pharmacy?

dialog.t: La farmàcia és a la plaça, davant de l'església.
dialog.tr: The pharmacy is on the square, across from the church.

dialog.t: Moltes gràcies!
dialog.tr: Thank you very much!

dialog.t: De res!
dialog.tr: You're welcome!

blocks.p: **Where, with {{ser}}.** To say where something is, Catalan uses {{ser}}, the verb of {{soc de Boston}}: {{On és l'estació?}} “Where's the station?” {{És a la plaça.}} “It's on the square.” For people you'll hear both {{ser}} and {{estar}} (lesson 9): {{Soc a casa}} and {{Estic a casa}} both mean “I'm at home”.

blocks.means: a little word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where: in, at, from, next to.

blocks.p: **{{a}} “in, at, to”.** {{a}} is the all-purpose word for places: {{a Barcelona}} “in Barcelona”, {{a la plaça}} “on the square”, {{a casa}} “at home”. With {{el}} it joins into one word: {{a}} + {{el}} = {{al}}: {{al mercat}} “at the market”. {{de}} and {{per}} “through, around” do the same. With {{la}} and {{l'}} nothing joins: {{a la plaça}}, {{de l'església}}.

table: on the right, on the left

ex.tr: The museum is near the harbor.

lessons.title: Say what there is
lessons.summary: Ask if there's a pharmacy nearby, and say what there is and isn't: “Is there a cash machine near here?”
lessons.topic: {{hi ha}} “there is, there are”; {{no hi ha}}, {{no hi ha cap}}; {{hi ha}} or {{és}}

goal.t: Hi ha una farmàcia a prop d'aquí?
goal.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

dialog.t: Hi ha wifi a l'habitació?
dialog.tr: Is there wifi in the room?

dialog.t: Sí, i la contrasenya és a la targeta.
dialog.tr: Yes, and the password is on the card.

dialog.tr: Yes, there's one right next door.

dialog.t: Sí, de set a deu, al menjador.

blocks.p: **{{hi ha}}** means both “there is” and “there are”: it never changes for the plural. {{Hi ha un bar.}} “There's a bar.” {{Hi ha dos bars.}} “There are two bars.” To ask, just raise your voice: {{Hi ha un bar a prop?}} “Is there a bar nearby?” For “there isn't”, put {{no}} in front: {{No hi ha pa.}} “There's no bread.” And with things you count, “no” is {{cap}}: {{No hi ha cap farmàcia.}} “There's no pharmacy.”

**The {{hi}}** is a little word meaning “there”, from the same family as {{em}} and {{et}}. In this phrase it always comes with {{ha}}, so learn {{hi ha}} as one block. You'll meet {{hi}} on its own in lesson 26.

**{{hi ha}} or {{és}}?** Use {{hi ha}} to say that something exists somewhere, usually with “a”, a number or nothing: {{Hi ha una farmàcia a la plaça.}} “There's a pharmacy on the square.” Use {{és}} to say where a particular thing is, with “the”: {{La farmàcia és a la plaça.}} “The pharmacy is on the square.”

lessons.title: Point, choose and pay in a shop
lessons.summary: Point at what you want, ask how much it is, and understand the price: “How much are these oranges?”
lessons.topic: {{aquest}} “this”, {{aquell}} “that”; {{això}}, {{allò}}; {{quin}} “which”; {{quant costa?}}; numbers

goal.t: Quant costen aquestes taronges?
goal.tr: How much are these oranges?

dialog.t: Bon dia! Què li poso?
dialog.tr: Good morning! What can I get you?

dialog.t: Bon dia. Quant costen aquestes taronges?
dialog.tr: Good morning. How much are these oranges?

dialog.t: Dos euros el quilo.
dialog.tr: Two euros a kilo.

dialog.t: Doncs un quilo, si us plau. I aquells tomàquets?
dialog.tr: A kilo, then, please. And those tomatoes?

dialog.t: Tres euros amb cinquanta.
dialog.tr: Three fifty.

dialog.t: D'acord, mig quilo. Quant és?
dialog.tr: OK, half a kilo. How much is that?

dialog.t: Són tres euros amb setanta-cinc.
dialog.tr: That's three seventy-five.

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{aquest}} is “this” (near you), {{aquell}} is “that” (over there). Like adjectives, they match the noun:
**{{això}} and {{allò}}** are “this” and “that” for something you don't name, or don't know the name of: {{Què és això?}} “What's this?” {{Quant costa això?}} “How much is this?”. They never change.

**Which one?** {{quin}} (feminine {{quina}}, plural {{quins}}, {{quines}}): {{Quin vols?}} “Which one do you want?” {{Aquest, si us plau.}} “This one, please.” On its own, {{aquest}} means “this one”.

**How much.** {{Quant costa?}} for one thing, {{Quant costen?}} for several. When you pay: {{Quant és?}} “How much is it (all)?”. Prices: {{dos euros amb cinquanta}} “two fifty” (€2.50), {{cinquanta cèntims}} “fifty cents”.

From 21 to 29 the numbers are joined with {{-i-}}: {{vint-i-u}}, {{vint-i-dos}}, {{vint-i-cinc}}. From 31 on, just a hyphen: {{trenta-u}}, {{quaranta-dos}}, {{setanta-cinc}}. When counting you say {{u}}; before a noun, {{un}} or {{una}}: {{vint-i-una cerveses}}.

ex.t: Quina vols, la vermella o la blava?
ex.tr: Which one do you want, the red one or the blue one?
ex.note: {{la vermella}} “the red one”: just the article and the adjective

blocks.tip: Paying: {{Puc pagar amb targeta?}} “Can I pay by card?”, or {{en efectiu}} “in cash”. In a shop you'll hear {{Alguna cosa més?}} “Anything else?”, and you answer {{Res més, gràcies}} “Nothing else, thanks”.

{{taronja}} is feminine: {{aquesta}}.
For a thing you don't name, “this” is {{això}}.

lessons.title: Say how you are and how things are
lessons.summary: Ask how someone is, say how you feel today, and tell apart what something is from how it is right now.
lessons.topic: {{estar}} for how you are: {{estic, estàs, està…}}; {{ser}} or {{estar}}

goal.t: Estic una mica cansada, però estic bé.
goal.tr: I'm a bit tired, but I'm fine.
goal.note: said by a woman; a man says {{cansat}}

dialog.t: Hola, Laia! Com estàs?
dialog.tr: Hi, Laia! How are you?

dialog.t: Bé, gràcies. Una mica cansada. I tu?
dialog.tr: Fine, thanks. A bit tired. And you?

dialog.t: Molt bé! Estic molt content: avui és divendres!
dialog.tr: Great! I'm really happy: it's Friday today!

dialog.t: I en Marc? Està millor?
dialog.tr: And Marc? Is he better?

dialog.t: Sí, ja està bé. Gràcies!
dialog.tr: Yes, he's fine now. Thanks!

blocks.p: **{{estar}}** is the other “to be”. It's for how someone or something is at the moment: how you feel, a state that comes and goes.

**{{ser}} or {{estar}}?** {{ser}} says what someone or something is: who, what kind, where from, what they're like. {{estar}} says how they are right now. Compare {{És avorrit.}} “He's boring.” with {{Està avorrit.}} “He's bored.”

table: {{La Marta és alegre.}} Marta is a cheerful person.
{{La Marta està contenta.}} Marta is happy (right now).
{{En Pau és de Vic.}} Pau is from Vic.
{{En Pau està malalt.}} Pau is sick.
{{La sopa és bona.}} The soup is good.
{{La sopa està freda.}} The soup is cold.

ex.note: {{tirant}}: a very Catalan “so-so”
{{llest}} “ready”; for a woman, {{llesta}}

blocks.tip: {{Com estàs?}} is for a friend; to someone you call {{vostè}}: {{Com està?}}. Quick and friendly: {{Com va?}} “How's it going?”, answered {{Bé!}}, {{Molt bé!}} or {{Tirant}}.

mistakes.why: Being tired comes and goes: {{estar}}.
Where someone is from is part of who they are: {{ser}}.

practice.why: {{estar}}: how he is right now, bored. “He's boring” is {{És avorrit.}}

practice.q: You meet a neighbor. Choose your replies.

She's tired: {{Que descansis!}} “Get some rest!” is kind. {{Que bé!}} is “Great!”.

Your turn: how are you today? And how is someone you know?

answers.tr: I'm really happy today: it's Saturday!

lessons.title: Say what you have, your age, and when you're hungry
lessons.summary: Say what you have and don't have, how old you are, and that you're hungry, thirsty or cold: “I'm twenty-five, and I'm really hungry!”
lessons.topic: {{tenir}} “to have”: {{tinc, tens, té…}}; {{tinc 25 anys}}; {{tinc gana, set, son, fred, calor}}

goal.t: Tinc vint-i-cinc anys i tinc molta gana!
goal.tr: I'm twenty-five, and I'm really hungry!

dialog.t: Uf, quina calor! Tens set?
dialog.tr: Phew, it's so hot! Are you thirsty?

dialog.t: Sí, molta. I tinc gana!
dialog.tr: Yes, very. And I'm hungry!

dialog.t: Tinc aigua i dos entrepans. Vols?
dialog.tr: I have water and two sandwiches. Do you want some?

dialog.t: Sí, gràcies! Ets molt amable.
dialog.tr: Yes, thanks! You're very kind.

blocks.p: **{{tenir}}** “to have”:

{{Tinc un germà.}} “I have a brother.” {{No tinc cotxe.}} “I don't have a car.” In questions and after {{no}}, something you'd normally have just one of goes without “a”: {{Tens cotxe?}} “Do you have a car?”, {{No tinc temps.}} “I don't have time.”
**Age with {{tenir}}.** In Catalan you “have” your years: {{Tinc trenta anys.}} “I'm thirty.” {{Quants anys tens?}} “How old are you?”, word for word “how many years do you have?”.

**Hungry, thirsty, cold: you “have” them too.** {{Tinc gana.}} “I'm hungry.” {{Tinc set.}} “I'm thirsty.” {{Tinc son.}} “I'm sleepy.” {{Tinc fred.}} “I'm cold.” {{Tinc calor.}} “I'm hot.” {{Tinc pressa.}} “I'm in a hurry.” {{Tinc por.}} “I'm scared.” They're nouns, so “very” is “a lot of”: {{Tinc molta gana}}, {{molta set}}, {{molta calor}}; with {{fred}}, {{molt de fred}}.

ex.tr: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
ex.note: {{germans}} covers brothers and sisters together

blocks.tip: {{té}} “has” keeps its accent: without it, {{te}} is “tea”.

mistakes.why: Age goes with {{tenir}}: “I have twenty years”.
Feeling cold is something you “have”: {{tinc fred}}. A cold thing takes {{estar}}: {{El cafè està fred.}} “The coffee is cold.”
{{gana}} is a feminine noun, so “a lot of” is {{molta}}.

practice.t: No vull res, gràcies. No ___ gana.
practice.tr: I don't want anything, thanks. I'm not hungry.
practice.why: {{tinc gana}} “I'm hungry”, word for word “I have hunger”.
{{son}} is sleepiness; “thirsty” is {{set}}, a hurry is {{pressa}}.

practice.q: On a hike with a friend. Choose your replies.

lines.why: Being kind is what someone is like: {{ser}}, {{ets}}.

practice.q: Say “Sorry, I'm in a hurry!” to a friend.
Your turn: how old are you, and how do you feel right now: hungry, thirsty, cold, sleepy?

answers.t: Tinc trenta-un anys i ara tinc una mica de son.
answers.tr: I'm thirty-one, and right now I'm a little sleepy.

answers.t: Tinc vint anys i tinc molta gana!
answers.tr: I'm twenty, and I'm really hungry!

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.summary: Say who's who in your family, and ask about someone else's: “My sister's name is Anna, and she has two kids.”
lessons.topic: {{el meu, la meva…}} “my”, {{el teu}} “your”, {{el seu}} “his, her, their”: possessives with the article

goal.t: La meva germana es diu Anna i té dos fills.
goal.tr: My sister's name is Anna, and she has two kids.

dialog.t: Aquesta és la teva família?
dialog.tr: Is this your family?

dialog.t: Sí! Aquests són els meus pares, i aquest és el meu germà petit.
dialog.tr: Yes! These are my parents, and this is my little brother.

dialog.t: I la noia?
dialog.tr: And the girl?

dialog.t: És la meva germana. Es diu Anna i té dos fills.
dialog.tr: That's my sister. Her name's Anna, and she has two kids.

dialog.t: I el seu marit?
dialog.tr: And her husband?

dialog.t: El seu marit és en Mark. És de Texas.
dialog.tr: Her husband is Mark. He's from Texas.

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **My, your… with “the”.** In Catalan, “my” comes with the article: {{el meu germà}}, word for word “the my brother”. And it matches the thing owned, not the owner: {{el meu pare}} “my father”, {{la meva mare}} “my mother”, {{els meus pares}} “my parents”, {{les meves amigues}} “my (female) friends”.

**His or her?** {{el seu}} is “his”, “her”, “their” and the polite “your”. It matches the thing, never the owner: {{la seva mare}} can be “his mother” or “her mother”, and the conversation makes it clear. Kate's sister's husband is {{el seu marit}}, masculine, because {{marit}} is.
**Names.** {{Es diu Anna}} “her name is Anna”: after {{em dic}} and {{et dius}} (lesson 1), {{es diu}} is the form for “he, she”.
As with {{germans}}, the masculine plural covers a mixed group: {{els pares}} “mother and father”, {{els fills}} “sons and daughters”, {{els avis}} “grandparents”.

ex.t: Els meus avis viuen a Reus.
Com es diu la teva parella?
La nostra filla té sis anys.
En Joan i la seva dona són molt simpàtics.
ex.tr: Joan and his wife are very nice.

ex.note: {{casa meva}} “my home”: with {{casa}}, the possessive goes after it, with no article

blocks.tip: The possessive can also follow the noun: {{un amic meu}} “a friend of mine”, {{una cosina meva}} “a cousin of mine”.

mistakes.why: “My” comes with the article: {{el meu}}.

mistakes.wrong: El meva mare és de Lleida.
mistakes.right: La meva mare és de Lleida.
mistakes.why: {{mare}} is feminine: {{la meva}}.

mistakes.wrong: La Kate és aquí amb la seva marit.
mistakes.right: La Kate és aquí amb el seu marit.
mistakes.tr: Kate is here with her husband.
mistakes.why: The possessive matches the husband (masculine), not Kate: {{el seu marit}} “her husband”.

practice.t: La Kate i el ___ marit són de Texas.
practice.tr: Kate and her husband are from Texas.
practice.why: {{seu}} matches {{marit}}, which is masculine, even though Kate is a woman.
The masculine plural covers a mixed group: brothers and sisters.

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your work, your studies and what you do every day: “I work in a shop, and I study Catalan in the evening.”
lessons.topic: The present tense of {{-ar}} verbs: {{parlo, parles, parla…}}

goal.t: Treballo en una botiga i estudio català al vespre.
goal.tr: I work in a shop, and I study Catalan in the evening.

dialog.t: A què et dediques?
dialog.tr: What do you do?

dialog.t: Treballo en un hotel. I tu?
dialog.tr: I work in a hotel. And you?

dialog.t: Jo estudio medicina i treballo els caps de setmana.
dialog.tr: I study medicine, and I work on weekends.

dialog.t: I parles anglès?
dialog.tr: And do you speak English?

dialog.t: Una mica. I tu parles molt bé el català!
dialog.tr: A little. And you speak Catalan really well!

dialog.t: Gràcies! Practico cada dia.
dialog.tr: Thanks! I practice every day.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to speak, to work. In Catalan it ends in {{-ar}}, {{-er}}, {{-re}} or {{-ir}}: {{parlar}}, {{tenir}}, {{viure}}, {{dormir}}.
the form of a verb that says when: the present (now, usually), the past, the future.

blocks.p: **The present.** Most Catalan verbs end in {{-ar}}: {{parlar}} “to speak”, {{treballar}} “to work”, {{estudiar}} “to study”. To use one, take off the {{-ar}} and add the ending for the person:

One Catalan present does the work of both English presents: {{Treballo aquí.}} is “I work here” and also “I'm working here (these days)”. And there's no “do” in questions: {{Treballes avui?}} “Are you working today?”, “Do you work today?”.

**Spelling keeps the sound.** Before an {{e}}, some letters change so that the verb sounds the same: {{menjar}} “to eat” gives {{menjo}}, but {{menges}}, {{mengem}}; {{començar}} “to start” gives {{comences}}; {{pagar}} “to pay”, {{pagues}}; {{trucar}} “to call”, {{truques}}.

ex.t: La Marta estudia a la universitat.

ex.tr: Where are you guys eating today?

ex.t: Els meus pares no parlen anglès.

ex.tr: Do you listen to music when you work?

ex.note: {{jo}} at the end puts the weight on “I”

blocks.tip: Everyday {{-ar}} verbs: {{parlar}} speak, {{treballar}} work, {{estudiar}} study, {{menjar}} eat, {{esmorzar}} have breakfast, {{dinar}} have lunch, {{sopar}} have dinner, {{comprar}} buy, {{escoltar}} listen, {{mirar}} look at, watch, {{tornar}} come back, {{arribar}} arrive, {{cuinar}} cook.

mistakes.why: For “I”, the ending is {{-o}}: {{treballo}}. And you don't need {{jo}}.
Before {{e}}, the {{j}} of {{menjar}} becomes {{g}}: {{menges}}.

lessons.title: Say where you live, what you read and what you drink
lessons.summary: Use the other kinds of verbs: “I live in Barcelona, and I read the paper every morning.”
lessons.topic: The present of {{-re}}, {{-er}} and {{-ir}} verbs: {{viure}}, {{beure}}, {{perdre}}, {{dormir}}, {{llegir}} (with {{-eix-}})

goal.t: Visc a Barcelona i llegeixo el diari cada matí.
goal.tr: I live in Barcelona, and I read the paper every morning.

dialog.t: On vius?
dialog.tr: Where do you live?

dialog.t: Visc a Sants, amb dues amigues.
dialog.tr: I live in Sants, with two friends.

dialog.t: I què fas els diumenges?
dialog.tr: And what do you do on Sundays?

dialog.t: Dormo molt! I llegeixo al parc.
dialog.tr: I sleep a lot! And I read in the park.

dialog.t: Què llegeixes ara?
dialog.tr: What are you reading at the moment?

dialog.t: Una novel·la en català. Entenc molt poc, però aprenc!

blocks.p: **Verbs in {{-re}} and {{-er}}.** Their endings are like those of {{-ar}} verbs, except for “you” and “he, she”: {{perdre}} “to lose” is {{perdo}}, {{perds}}, {{perd}}, {{perdem}}, {{perdeu}}, {{perden}}.

Many common ones are a little irregular, with a {{-c}} for “I”: {{viure}} “to live”, {{visc}}; {{beure}} “to drink”, {{bec}}; {{entendre}} “to understand”, {{entenc}}; {{aprendre}} “to learn”, {{aprenc}}; {{conèixer}} “to know (a person, a place)”, {{conec}}.

**Verbs in {{-ir}}.** A few, like {{dormir}} “to sleep”, are simple: {{dormo}}, {{dorms}}, {{dorm}}, {{dormim}}, {{dormiu}}, {{dormen}}. Most add {{-eix-}} in four of the six forms, like {{llegir}} “to read”:

ex.note: {{t'}} “you”: the little word {{et}} before a vowel

ex.tr: We read the paper every morning.
I know a really good restaurant.

blocks.tip: To know a fact is {{saber}} ({{sé}} “I know”); to know a person or a place is {{conèixer}} ({{conec}}): {{No sé on viu.}} “I don't know where she lives.” {{Conec la seva germana.}} “I know her sister.”

mistakes.why: {{viure}} is irregular: “I live” is {{visc}}.
{{llegir}} takes {{-eix-}}: {{llegeixo}}.
To know a person is {{conèixer}}; {{saber}} is for facts.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like and don't like, ask others, and agree: “I really like coffee, but I don't like cookies.”
lessons.topic: {{m'agrada}} and {{m'agraden}}; {{em, et, li, ens, us, els}} “to me, to you…”; {{a mi també}}, {{a mi tampoc}}

goal.t: M'agrada molt el cafè, però no m'agraden les galetes.
goal.tr: I really like coffee, but I don't like cookies.

dialog.t: T'agrada el futbol?
dialog.tr: Do you like soccer?

dialog.t: No gaire. M'agrada més el bàsquet.
dialog.tr: Not really. I like basketball better.

dialog.t: A mi també m'agrada el bàsquet! I t'agraden les pel·lícules de por?
dialog.tr: I like basketball too! And do you like horror movies?

dialog.t: No, no m'agraden gens!
dialog.tr: No, I don't like them at all!

dialog.t: A mi tampoc. Prefereixo les comèdies.
dialog.tr: Me neither. I prefer comedies.

blocks.p: **Back to front.** {{M'agrada el cafè}} is, word for word, “coffee pleases me”: the thing you like does the verb, and you are the little word {{em}} “to me” in front of it ({{m'}} before a vowel). So the verb goes with the thing: one thing, {{m'agrada}}; several, {{m'agraden}}.

blocks.means: one of Catalan's little unstressed words for people and things, like {{em}} “me, to me”, {{et}} “you, to you” or {{hi}} “there”. They lean on the verb, usually just before it.

blocks.p: **With “the”.** Things you like in general take the article: {{M'agrada el cafè.}} “I like coffee.” {{M'agraden els gats.}} “I like cats.” To like doing something, add a verb in the infinitive, and keep {{agrada}}: {{M'agrada cuinar.}} “I like cooking.”

**Saying who, and agreeing.** To make it clear who, or to compare, put {{a mi}}, {{a tu}}, {{a ell}}, {{a la Marta}}… in front: {{A la Marta li agrada el jazz.}} “Marta likes jazz.” {{A mi també.}} “Me too.” After a “not”: {{A mi tampoc.}} “Me neither.” How much: {{molt}} “a lot”, {{bastant}} “quite”, {{no gaire}} “not much”, {{gens}} “at all”; and {{m'encanta}} “I love it”.

ex.note: {{molt}} “a lot”

ex.t: Al meu fill li agraden els dinosaures.

ex.tr: I don't like the cold at all.

ex.t: Us agrada el pa amb tomàquet?
ex.tr: Do you guys like pa amb tomàquet?
ex.note: bread rubbed with tomato and olive oil: Catalonia's favorite

blocks.tip: {{m'encanta}} works like {{m'agrada}}: {{M'encanten les platges de la Costa Brava.}} “I love the beaches of the Costa Brava.” With a person, {{m'agrada}} sounds romantic; to say you like someone as a person, use {{em cau bé}}: {{La teva germana em cau molt bé.}} “I really like your sister.”

mistakes.why: Several things: the verb is plural, {{m'agraden}}.
The thing does the verb, “coffee pleases me”: {{m'agrada}}.
Things in general take the article: {{el cafè}}.

lessons.title: Say where you're going and what you're doing
lessons.summary: Say where you're off to and ask what someone is up to: “I'm going to the movies this afternoon. What are you doing?”
lessons.topic: {{anar}} “to go”: {{vaig, vas, va…}} + {{a}}; {{fer}} “to do, to make”: {{faig, fas, fa…}}

goal.t: Aquesta tarda vaig al cinema. I tu, què fas?
goal.tr: I'm going to the movies this afternoon. What about you, what are you doing?

dialog.t: Ei, què fas?
dialog.tr: Hey, what are you up to?

dialog.t: Res especial. I tu?
dialog.tr: Nothing special. You?

dialog.t: Vaig a la platja amb la Laia. Vens?
dialog.tr: I'm going to the beach with Laia. Are you coming?

dialog.t: Sí! On aneu, a la Barceloneta?
dialog.tr: Yes! Where are you going, to Barceloneta?

dialog.t: Sí. Anem en bici.
dialog.tr: Yes. We're going by bike.

dialog.t: Perfecte, ara vinc!
dialog.tr: Great, I'm on my way!

blocks.p: **{{anar}} “to go”** is irregular, and worth learning well: in lesson 24 it does something surprising.

**Where to.** After {{anar}}, the place takes {{a}} ({{al}}, {{a la}}, {{als}}…): {{Vaig a Girona.}} “I'm going to Girona.” {{Vas al mercat?}} “Are you going to the market?” {{Anem a casa.}} “We're going home.” The present is enough for where you're going now or soon: {{Demà vaig a Sitges.}} “I'm going to Sitges tomorrow.”
**How.** {{a peu}} “on foot”, {{en cotxe}} “by car”, {{en tren}} “by train”, {{en metro}} “by subway”, {{en bici}} “by bike”.

**{{fer}}** is both “to do” and “to make”: {{Què fas?}} “What are you doing?” or “What do you do?”; {{Faig el sopar.}} “I'm making dinner.” It turns up in many everyday phrases: {{fer un cafè}} “have a coffee (out)”, {{fer esport}} “do sports”, {{fer una passejada}} “go for a walk”, {{fer la compra}} “do the grocery shopping”.

lessons.title: Talk about the weather
lessons.summary: Say what the weather is like, and make small talk: “It's really hot today, isn't it?”
lessons.topic: {{fa}} + {{calor, fred, sol, vent}}; {{plou}}, {{neva}}; {{està ennuvolat}}; no word for “it”

goal.t: Avui fa molta calor, oi?
goal.tr: It's really hot today, isn't it?

dialog.t: Bon dia! Quin temps més bo, oi?
dialog.tr: Good morning! Lovely weather, isn't it?

dialog.t: Sí, fa molt de sol. Però fa una mica de vent.
dialog.tr: Yes, it's very sunny. But it's a bit windy.

dialog.t: Ah, sí? Doncs agafo el paraigua!

blocks.p: **No “it”.** Catalan talks about the weather with no word for “it”: {{Plou.}} “It's raining.” {{Fa fred.}} “It's cold.” Most weather goes with {{fa}} (from {{fer}}, lesson 15): word for word, “(it) makes cold”.

**How much.** {{calor}}, {{fred}}, {{sol}} and {{vent}} are nouns, so “very” is “a lot of”: {{Fa molta calor.}} “It's very hot.” {{Fa molt de fred.}} “It's very cold.” {{Fa molt de vent.}} “It's very windy.” ({{calor}} is feminine: {{molta calor}}.) To ask: {{Quin temps fa?}} “What's the weather like?”.
**Feeling it.** The weather {{fa}}; you {{tens}} (lesson 10): {{Fa fred i tinc fred.}} “It's cold, and I'm cold.”

ex.tr: What's the weather like in London?
It rains a lot in winter.

blocks.tip: The seasons: {{la primavera}} spring, {{l'estiu}} summer, {{la tardor}} fall, {{l'hivern}} winter. “In summer” is {{a l'estiu}}.

{{calor}} is a feminine noun: {{molta calor}}.

lessons.title: Describe your daily routine
lessons.summary: Walk someone through your day: “I get up at seven, I have a shower, and then I have breakfast.”
lessons.topic: Verbs with {{em, et, es…}} for things you do to yourself ({{em llevo}}, {{em dutxo}}); {{soler}} + a verb “usually”; {{primer}}, {{després}}

goal.t: Em llevo a les set, em dutxo i després esmorzo.
goal.tr: I get up at seven, I have a shower, and then I have breakfast.

dialog.t: A quina hora et lleves?
dialog.tr: What time do you get up?

dialog.t: Normalment em llevo a les sis i mitja.
dialog.tr: Normally I get up at six thirty.

dialog.t: Tan d'hora? Jo em llevo a les nou!
dialog.tr: That early? I get up at nine!

dialog.t: És que començo a treballar a les vuit.
dialog.tr: Well, I start work at eight.

dialog.t: I a quina hora vas a dormir?
dialog.tr: And what time do you go to bed?

dialog.t: Solc anar a dormir a les onze.
dialog.tr: I usually go to bed at eleven.

blocks.means: a verb used with a little word for the same person who does it, as if you did it to yourself: {{em llevo}} “I get (myself) up”. In the dictionary it has {{-se}} on the end: {{llevar-se}}.

blocks.p: **Doing it to yourself.** Many routine verbs come with a weak pronoun meaning “myself, yourself…”. It goes just before the verb and changes with the person: {{em llevo}}, {{et lleves}}, {{es lleva}}… You already know one: {{em dic}} (lesson 1).

Before a vowel, {{em}}, {{et}} and {{es}} become {{m'}}, {{t'}}, {{s'}}: {{m'afaito}} “I shave”, {{s'aixeca}} “she gets up”. More routine verbs like these: {{despertar-se}} “to wake up”, {{vestir-se}} “to get dressed” ({{em vesteixo}}), {{rentar-se}} “to wash”, {{pentinar-se}} “to comb your hair”.

**Usually.** {{soler}} + a verb is “to usually do”: {{Solc dinar a les dues.}} “I usually have lunch at two.” Its forms: {{solc}}, {{sols}}, {{sol}}, {{solem}}, {{soleu}}, {{solen}}. Or simply {{normalment}} “normally”, {{sempre}} “always”.

**In order.** {{primer}} “first”, {{després}} “then, afterwards”, {{al final}} “in the end”. The parts of the day: {{al matí}} “in the morning”, {{al migdia}} “at midday”, {{a la tarda}} “in the afternoon”, {{al vespre}} “in the evening”, {{a la nit}} “at night”.

ex.t: Em desperto a les set, però no em llevo fins a les set i quart.
ex.tr: I wake up at seven, but I don't get up until a quarter past.
The kids get dressed by themselves.
Do you usually have breakfast at home?

ex.t: Al migdia dino a la feina.
ex.tr: At midday I have lunch at work.

ex.t: Primer em rento les dents i després em vesteixo.
ex.tr: First I brush my teeth, and then I get dressed.
ex.note: {{les dents}} “the teeth”: for your own body, Catalan says “the”, not “my”

blocks.tip: Meals: {{l'esmorzar}} “breakfast”, {{el dinar}} “lunch” (the big meal, around two), {{el berenar}} “afternoon snack”, {{el sopar}} “dinner” (often at nine or later). Each is also a verb: {{Dinem?}} “Shall we have lunch?”.

mistakes.why: {{llevar-se}} needs its pronoun: {{em llevo}}. Without it, {{llevar}} means “to take away”.
For your own body Catalan says “the”: {{les dents}}. The {{em}} already says whose.
For “you”, the pronoun is {{et}}: {{et lleves}}.

lessons.title: Tell the time and arrange to meet
lessons.summary: Ask and tell the time, say when things happen, and set up a meeting: “Shall we meet on Saturday at ten?”
lessons.topic: {{Quina hora és?}}; {{és la una}}, {{són les dues}}; {{a les cinc}}; the Catalan quarter clock; the days of the week

goal.t: Quedem dissabte a les deu?
goal.tr: Shall we meet on Saturday at ten?

dialog.t: Quedem per fer un cafè?
dialog.tr: Shall we meet for a coffee?

dialog.t: Sí! Quan et va bé?
dialog.tr: Yes! When suits you?

dialog.t: Dissabte al matí?
dialog.tr: Saturday morning?

dialog.t: Perfecte. A quina hora?
dialog.tr: Perfect. What time?

dialog.t: A les deu i mitja, a la plaça del Sol.
dialog.tr: At ten thirty, in Plaça del Sol.

dialog.t: D'acord. Fins dissabte!
dialog.tr: OK. See you Saturday!

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{Quina hora és?}} One o'clock is singular, the others plural: {{És la una.}} “It's one o'clock.” {{Són les dues.}} “It's two.” {{Són les deu.}} “It's ten.” The {{les}} stands for {{les hores}} “the hours”, so it's feminine: {{les dues}}, not {{els dos}}.

**At what time?** {{A quina hora?}}: {{a la una}}, {{a les cinc}}. In everyday speech, especially with digital clocks: {{les cinc i quart}} (5:15), {{les cinc i mitja}} (5:30), {{les sis menys quart}} (5:45), {{les cinc i deu}} (5:10).

**The Catalan quarter clock.** Many Catalans, in Barcelona too, count quarters towards the next hour, like a church bell: {{un quart de sis}}, “one quarter of the way to six”, is 5:15; {{dos quarts de sis}} is 5:30; {{tres quarts de sis}} is 5:45. You don't have to use it, but you'll hear it all the time.

**Days.** {{dilluns}} Monday, {{dimarts}} Tuesday, {{dimecres}} Wednesday, {{dijous}} Thursday, {{divendres}} Friday, {{dissabte}} Saturday, {{diumenge}} Sunday, all with a small letter. There's no word for “on”: {{dissabte}} alone means “(this) Saturday”, and {{els dissabtes}} “on Saturdays, every Saturday”.

ex.tr: Excuse me, what time is it?

ex.t: La botiga obre a les nou.
Ens veiem a dos quarts de vuit.
ex.note: {{ens veiem}} “we see each other”

ex.t: Els dimarts tinc classe de català.
ex.tr: On Tuesdays I have Catalan class.

ex.t: Dijous no puc, però divendres sí.
ex.tr: Thursday I can't, but Friday I can.

blocks.tip: {{quedar}} is the word for arranging to meet: {{Quedem?}} “Shall we meet up?”, {{Quedem a les vuit?}} “Shall we meet at eight?”. {{Quan et va bé?}} “When suits you?” is the friendly way to ask.

mistakes.why: One o'clock is singular: {{és la una}}.
Hours are feminine ({{les hores}}): {{les dues}}.
There's no word for “on” before a day: just {{dilluns}}.

lessons.title: Say what you can and want to do
lessons.summary: Ask if you can do something, and say what you want to do and what you know how to do: “Can I pay by card?”
lessons.topic: {{poder}} “can”, {{voler}} “want” and {{saber}} “know how to” + an infinitive

goal.t: Puc pagar amb targeta?
goal.tr: Can I pay by card?

dialog.t: Vols venir a la platja diumenge?
dialog.tr: Do you want to come to the beach on Sunday?

dialog.t: Vull, però no puc: treballo.
dialog.tr: I'd like to, but I can't: I'm working.

dialog.t: I dissabte? Podem anar en caiac!
dialog.tr: And Saturday? We can go kayaking!

dialog.t: Dissabte sí que puc. Però no sé remar…
dialog.tr: Saturday I can. But I don't know how to paddle…

dialog.t: No passa res, t'ensenyo jo!
dialog.tr: No problem, I'll teach you!

blocks.p: **Verb + verb.** {{poder}} “can, be able to”, {{voler}} “want” and {{saber}} “know how to” are followed straight by a second verb in the infinitive, with nothing between them: {{Puc venir.}} “I can come.” {{Vull aprendre.}} “I want to learn.” {{Sé nedar.}} “I can swim (I know how).”

**Can: {{poder}} or {{saber}}?** English “can” has two jobs. For a skill you've learned, Catalan uses {{saber}}: {{Saps cuinar?}} “Can you cook?”. For being able, free or allowed right now, it's {{poder}}: {{Avui no puc cuinar, no tinc temps.}} “I can't cook today, I don't have time.”

**Asking.** {{Puc…?}} “Can I…?” asks for permission: {{Puc obrir la finestra?}} “Can I open the window?”. {{Pots…?}} “Can you…?” asks someone to do something: {{Pots parlar més a poc a poc?}} “Can you speak more slowly?”.

ex.tr: Do you want to come with us?

ex.note: a skill: {{saber}}

ex.t: Pots parlar més a poc a poc, si us plau?

blocks.tip: Two phrases you'll hear every day: {{No pot ser!}} “It can't be!”, “No way!”, and {{No passa res}} “It doesn't matter”, “No problem”.

A skill you've learned is {{saber}}.

lessons.title: Say what you have to do
lessons.summary: Say what you have to do, what's necessary and what isn't: “Tomorrow I have to work until eight.”
lessons.topic: {{haver de}} + infinitive “have to”: {{he de, has de, ha de…}}; {{cal}}, {{no cal}}

goal.t: Demà he de treballar fins a les vuit.
goal.tr: Tomorrow I have to work until eight.

dialog.t: Vens a sopar aquesta nit?
dialog.tr: Are you coming to dinner tonight?

dialog.t: No puc, he d'estudiar. Demà tinc un examen.
dialog.tr: I can't, I have to study. I have an exam tomorrow.

dialog.t: I dissabte?
dialog.tr: And Saturday?

dialog.t: Dissabte sí. Haig de portar alguna cosa?
dialog.tr: Saturday, yes. Do I need to bring anything?

dialog.t: No, no cal. Només has de venir!
dialog.tr: No, there's no need. You just have to come!

blocks.p: **{{haver de}}** + an infinitive is “have to, must”. It's the {{haver}} of {{hi ha}}, with {{de}} before the second verb:

table: {{He de marxar.}} I have to go.
{{Has de venir!}} You have to come!
{{Ha de treballar.}} She has to work.
{{Hem de parlar.}} We need to talk.
{{Han de pagar.}} They have to pay.

blocks.p: {{de}} becomes {{d'}} before a vowel: {{he d'estudiar}}, {{has d'anar}}. For “I have to”, {{haig de}} is very common in speech; both are correct.

**It's necessary: {{cal}}.** For something necessary in general, not for one person, use {{cal}} + an infinitive: {{Cal reservar taula.}} “You need to book a table.” {{No cal}} is “there's no need”: {{No cal pagar.}} “You don't have to pay.” On its own, {{No cal!}} means “No need!”.

ex.t: Has de provar el pa amb tomàquet.
ex.tr: You have to try pa amb tomàquet.

ex.t: Demà ens hem de llevar molt d'hora.
ex.tr: We have to get up very early tomorrow.
ex.note: the {{ens}} of {{llevar-se}} goes in front of {{hem de}}

ex.tr: Do you need to bring your passport?
What do I have to do?

blocks.tip: “I have to” is never {{tinc que}} in good Catalan, though you may hear it: it's a borrowing careful speakers avoid. Say {{he de}} or {{haig de}}.

mistakes.why: “Have to” is {{haver de}}: {{he de}}.
Don't forget the {{de}}: {{he de}}.

practice.tr: We have to get up very early tomorrow.

lessons.title: Make plans and suggestions
lessons.summary: Suggest doing something, say what you're planning, and accept or turn down an invitation: “Do you feel like going to the movies on Saturday?”
lessons.topic: The present for plans ({{demà treballo}}); {{pensar}} + infinitive “plan to”; {{et ve de gust…?}}; {{per què no…?}}; {{em sap greu}}

goal.t: Et ve de gust anar al cinema dissabte?
goal.tr: Do you feel like going to the movies on Saturday?

dialog.t: Què fas aquest cap de setmana?
dialog.tr: What are you doing this weekend?

dialog.t: Dissabte treballo, però diumenge estic lliure.
dialog.tr: I'm working on Saturday, but Sunday I'm free.

dialog.t: Penso anar a Montserrat. Et ve de gust venir?
dialog.tr: I'm planning to go to Montserrat. Do you feel like coming?

dialog.t: Sí, amb molt de gust! Anem en tren?
dialog.tr: Yes, I'd love to! Shall we go by train?

dialog.t: Sí, el tren surt a les nou de plaça d'Espanya.
dialog.tr: Yes, the train leaves at nine from Plaça d'Espanya.

dialog.t: Perfecte. Quedem a tres quarts de nou a l'estació?
dialog.tr: Perfect. Shall we meet at a quarter to nine at the station?

dialog.t: Fet!
dialog.tr: Deal!

blocks.p: **The present for plans.** Catalan often talks about plans with the plain present and a time word: {{Dissabte treballo.}} “I'm working on Saturday.” {{Demà anem a la platja.}} “We're going to the beach tomorrow.” {{Què fas aquest cap de setmana?}} “What are you doing this weekend?”

**Planning to.** {{pensar}} + an infinitive is “to plan to, to be thinking of”: {{Penso anar a Montserrat.}} “I'm planning to go to Montserrat.” Or use {{voler}}: {{Vull fer una festa.}} “I want to have a party.”

**Suggesting.** The most Catalan way is {{Et ve de gust…?}} “Do you feel like…?”, word for word “does it come to you with pleasure?”; to several people, {{Us ve de gust…?}}. Others: {{Per què no…?}} “Why don't we…?”, or just the “we” form: {{Sopem fora?}} “Shall we eat out?”. {{Anem!}} on its own is “Let's go!”.

table: {{Et ve de gust anar a la platja?}}

blocks.p: **{{Em sap greu}}** “I'm sorry”, word for word “it weighs on me”, is how Catalans turn something down kindly. You'll hear it all the time.

ex.t: Aquest estiu pensem anar a Itàlia.
ex.tr: This summer we're planning to go to Italy.

ex.t: Per què no sopem a casa meva?

ex.t: Em sap greu, aquest dissabte no em va bé.
ex.tr: I'm sorry, this Saturday doesn't work for me.

blocks.tip: Catalan avoids {{anar a}} + a verb for the future. Plans are the present ({{Dissabte vaig a la platja.}}), {{pensar}} + a verb, or the future tense (lesson 37). {{Vaig a}} + a verb is for going somewhere to do something: {{Vaig a comprar pa.}} “I'm off to buy bread.”

lessons.summary: Say “it” and “them” the Catalan way, before the verb: “I don't know, I can't find it.”
lessons.topic: {{el, la, l', els, les}} “it, him, her, them” and {{ho}} “it, that”: before the verb, or after an infinitive ({{comprar-lo}})

goal.t: No ho sé, no la trobo.

blocks.means: the person or thing a verb acts on: in “I buy the sweater”, the sweater is the object.

blocks.p: **“It” is a weak pronoun.** To avoid repeating an object, Catalan uses {{el}}, {{la}}, {{els}}, {{les}}, which look just like the articles. They match the noun's gender and number, and they go right before the verb: {{Compro el jersei.}} → {{El compro.}} “I'll buy it.” {{Conec la Marta.}} → {{La conec.}} “I know her.”
Before a vowel, {{el}} and {{la}} become {{l'}}: {{L'espero aquí.}} “I'll wait for him (or her) here.”

**{{ho}}** is “it” or “that” for something that isn't a noun: a fact, an idea, what someone has just said. {{No ho sé.}} “I don't know.” {{Ho entenc.}} “I understand.” {{Ho sento.}} “I'm sorry”, word for word “I feel it”.

**With an infinitive.** With two verbs, the pronoun can go before both, or on the end of the infinitive with a hyphen: {{El vull comprar.}} = {{Vull comprar-lo.}} “I want to buy it.” On the end, {{el}} becomes {{-lo}} and {{els}} becomes {{-los}}; {{-la}}, {{-les}} and {{-ho}} stay the same.

lessons.title: Ask for amounts: some, none, how many
lessons.summary: Ask for a quantity, and say you have some or none, without repeating the thing: “Apples? Yes, I'd like a kilo, please.”
lessons.topic: {{en}} “of it, of them, some”: {{en vull dos}}, {{no en tinc}}; {{molt, poc, una mica, massa, prou, gaire}}

goal.t: Pomes? Sí, en vull un quilo, si us plau.
goal.tr: Apples? Yes, I'd like a kilo, please.

dialog.t: Què et poso?
dialog.tr: What can I get you?

dialog.t: Sí. Quants en vols?

blocks.p: **{{en}}: some of it, of them.** When you talk about an amount of something already mentioned, Catalan uses the weak pronoun {{en}}, before the verb: {{Vols pa? —Sí, en vull.}} “Do you want some bread? —Yes, I'd like some.” {{Quants germans tens? —En tinc dos.}} “How many brothers and sisters do you have? —I have two.” English often says nothing here (“I have two”), but Catalan needs its {{en}}.

Before a vowel it becomes {{n'}}: {{N'hi ha molts.}} “There are lots (of them).” That's the {{n'}} of {{n'hi ha un}} in lesson 7. On the end of an infinitive it becomes {{-ne}}: {{Vull comprar-ne.}} “I want to buy some.”

**How much.** {{molt}} “a lot, many” and {{poc}} “little, few” agree with the noun like adjectives: {{molta gent}} “a lot of people”, {{molts amics}} “lots of friends”, {{pocs diners}} “little money”. {{massa}} “too much, too many” and {{prou}} “enough” never change: {{massa feina}} “too much work”, {{prou temps}} “enough time”. {{una mica}} “a little” takes {{de}}: {{una mica de llet}} “a little milk”.
**{{gaire}}** is “much, many” after {{no}} and in questions: {{No tinc gaire temps.}} “I don't have much time.” {{Hi ha gaire gent?}} “Are there many people?”

ex.tr: Do you have kids? —Yes, I have two.

ex.t: Vols més cafè? —No, gràcies, encara en tinc.
ex.tr: More coffee? —No, thanks, I still have some.

ex.tr: Do we have enough chairs? —No, we're two short.

blocks.tip: {{els diners}} “money” is plural in Catalan: {{No tinc diners.}} “I don't have any money.” {{Tinc pocs diners.}} “I have little money.”

lessons.title: Say what happened yesterday
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday, last week or last year, with Catalan's own past: “Yesterday I went to the beach with some friends.”
lessons.topic: The past with {{anar}}: {{vaig, vas, va, vam, vau, van}} + infinitive; {{vaig anar}} “I went” or {{vaig a…}} “I'm going to…”

goal.t: Ahir vaig anar a la platja amb uns amics.
goal.tr: Yesterday I went to the beach with some friends.

dialog.t: Què vas fer ahir?
dialog.tr: What did you do yesterday?

dialog.t: Vaig anar a la platja amb uns amics.
dialog.tr: I went to the beach with some friends.

dialog.t: Que bé! Vau menjar allà?
dialog.tr: Nice! Did you eat there?

dialog.t: Sí, vam dinar en un xiringuito i després vam nedar.
dialog.tr: Yes, we had lunch at a beach bar, and then we went swimming.

dialog.tr: And what time did you get back?

dialog.t: Vam tornar molt tard. Avui estic mort!
dialog.tr: We got back really late. I'm dead today!

blocks.p: **A surprise.** To tell what happened, Catalan takes the present of {{anar}} “to go” (lesson 15) and adds the infinitive of the verb: {{vaig}} “I go” + {{menjar}} “to eat” = {{vaig menjar}} “I ate”. There's no going in it any more: it's simply the past.

blocks.means: a helper verb that goes with another verb to make a tense: in “I have eaten”, “have” is the auxiliary.

table: {{Vaig parlar amb ella.}} I spoke to her.
{{Vas anar a la festa?}} Did you go to the party?
{{Va fer molt de fred.}} It was very cold.
{{Vam sopar a casa.}} We had dinner at home.
{{Vau veure el partit?}} Did you guys see the game?

blocks.p: **The good news:** every verb works the same way, regular or not. Learn the six helpers and you can put any verb you know into the past: {{vaig ser}} “I was”, {{vaig tenir}} “I had”, {{vaig veure}} “I saw”. Note that “we” and “you” aren't the present forms: {{vam}}, {{vau}} (the present is {{anem}}, {{aneu}}).

**When.** Use it for things that happened at a time that's over: {{ahir}} “yesterday”, {{la setmana passada}} “last week”, {{l'any passat}} “last year”, {{dilluns}} “on Monday”, {{el 2015}} “in 2015”. For today, Catalan has another past (lesson 25).
**{{vaig}} or {{vaig a}}?** Watch the little {{a}}. {{Vaig comprar pa.}} “I bought bread.” {{Vaig a comprar pa.}} “I'm going (out) to buy bread.” With the {{a}}, it's real going again.

lessons.title: Say what you've done today
lessons.summary: Talk about today, this morning or this week with the other past: “I've worked a lot today, and I still haven't had lunch.”
lessons.topic: The {{perfet}}: {{he, has, ha, hem, heu, han}} + participle ({{-at, -ut, -it}}); today or yesterday

goal.t: Avui he treballat molt i encara no he dinat.
goal.tr: I've worked a lot today, and I still haven't had lunch.

dialog.t: Com ha anat el dia?
dialog.tr: How was your day?

dialog.t: Bé, però he treballat molt. I tu?
dialog.tr: Fine, but I've worked a lot. And you?

dialog.t: Aquest matí he anat al mercat i he fet una paella.

dialog.t: Que bé! N'has deixat una mica per a mi?
dialog.tr: Great! Have you left some for me?

dialog.t: És clar! Vols sopar ara?
dialog.tr: Of course! Do you want to have dinner now?

dialog.t: Sí, que avui encara no he menjat res!
dialog.tr: Yes, I haven't eaten anything today!

blocks.p: **Catalan has two pasts.** The past with {{anar}} (lesson 24) is for a time that's over: yesterday, last week. For a time that isn't over yet (today, this morning, this week, this year) Catalan uses the {{perfet}}, {{he}} + a participle, like English “I have worked”: {{Avui he treballat molt.}} “I've worked a lot today.” {{Ahir vaig treballar molt.}} “Yesterday I worked a lot.”

blocks.means: the form of a verb used after “have”: worked, eaten, done. In Catalan it mostly ends in {{-at}}, {{-ut}} or {{-it}}.

blocks.p: **Participles.** {{-ar}} verbs end in {{-at}} ({{parlat}}, {{menjat}}); most {{-er}} and {{-re}} verbs in {{-ut}} ({{perdut}} “lost”, {{begut}} “drunk”, {{viscut}} “lived”, {{tingut}} “had”, {{pogut}}, {{volgut}}); {{-ir}} verbs in {{-it}} ({{dormit}}, {{llegit}}). Some common ones are irregular:

**Already, not yet.** {{ja}} “already”, {{encara no}} “not yet”: {{Ja he dinat.}} “I've already had lunch.” {{Encara no he dinat.}} “I haven't had lunch yet.” Nothing goes between {{he}} and the participle: {{he dinat}}, {{no he dinat}}.

ex.t: Aquest matí he anat al metge.
ex.tr: I went to the doctor this morning.
ex.note: English uses its simple past here; Catalan uses the {{perfet}} for anything today

ex.tr: We've worked a lot this week.

ex.note: just now: the {{perfet}}

ex.tr: The kids have already had dinner.

ex.t: Encara no he fet els deures.
ex.tr: I haven't done my homework yet.

blocks.tip: {{Com ha anat?}} “How did it go?” is the question for something that has just happened: {{Com ha anat l'examen?}} “How did the exam go?”.

mistakes.tr: I went to the movies yesterday.

lessons.title: Talk about your experiences
lessons.summary: Ask if someone has ever done something, and say what you've done or never done: “Have you ever been to Menorca? —Yes, I've been there twice.”
lessons.topic: {{Has … mai…?}} “Have you ever…?”; {{mai}}, {{ja}}, {{encara no}}; {{hi}} “there”: {{hi he estat}}

goal.t: Has estat mai a Menorca?
goal.tr: Have you ever been to Menorca?

dialog.t: Has estat mai a Menorca?
dialog.tr: Have you ever been to Menorca?

dialog.t: No, mai. I tu?
dialog.tr: No, never. And you?

dialog.t: Sí, hi he estat moltes vegades. Hi tinc família.
dialog.tr: Yes, I've been there lots of times. I have family there.

dialog.t: I has menjat mai caldereta de llagosta?
dialog.tr: And have you ever eaten lobster stew?

dialog.t: Sí, una vegada. És caríssima, però boníssima!
dialog.tr: Yes, once. It's really expensive, but delicious!

dialog.t: Doncs l'estiu que ve hi vull anar!
dialog.tr: Well, I want to go there next summer!

blocks.p: **Ever.** For experiences up to now, Catalan uses the {{perfet}} (lesson 25): your life isn't over! “Ever” is {{mai}}: {{Has estat mai a Roma?}} “Have you ever been to Rome?”. In an answer, {{mai}} is “never”, with {{no}} before the verb: {{No hi he estat mai.}} “I've never been there.”
**How many times.** {{una vegada}} “once”, {{dues vegades}} “twice”, {{moltes vegades}} “many times”; in speech also {{un cop}}, {{dos cops}}.

**{{hi}}: there.** To avoid repeating a place, Catalan uses the weak pronoun {{hi}} “there”, before the verb: {{Has estat a Menorca? —Sí, hi he estat.}} “Have you been to Menorca? —Yes, I've been there.” It's the same {{hi}} as in {{hi ha}} (lesson 7), and it stands for a place with {{a}}, {{en}} or {{al}}: {{Vas a la platja? —Sí, hi vaig ara.}} “Are you going to the beach? —Yes, I'm going now.” On the end of an infinitive: {{Vull anar-hi.}} “I want to go there.”

Hem estat a Londres tres vegades.
ex.tr: We've been to London three times.

ex.t: Coneixes Girona? —Sí, hi he estat un cop.
ex.tr: Do you know Girona? —Yes, I've been there once.
Have you finished the book yet?

Without the place, Catalan needs {{hi}} “there”.

lessons.title: Say how long ago and how long
lessons.summary: Say when something happened and how long it has been going on: “I've been living in Barcelona for three years.”
lessons.topic: {{fa}} + a time “ago”; {{fa … que}} and {{des de fa}} “for”; {{des de}} “since”; dates

goal.t: Fa tres anys que visc a Barcelona.
goal.tr: I've been living in Barcelona for three years.

dialog.t: Quant de temps fa que vius aquí?
dialog.tr: How long have you been living here?

dialog.t: Fa tres anys. Vaig venir per feina.
dialog.tr: Three years. I came for work.

dialog.t: I quan vas començar a estudiar català?
dialog.tr: And when did you start learning Catalan?

dialog.t: Fa un any. Estudio català des del setembre passat.
dialog.tr: A year ago. I've been studying Catalan since last September.

dialog.t: Doncs el parles molt bé!
dialog.tr: Well, you speak it really well!

blocks.p: **Ago.** {{fa}} + a length of time means “… ago”: {{Vaig arribar fa tres anys.}} “I arrived three years ago.” {{La vaig veure fa una setmana.}} “I saw her a week ago.” It's {{fer}} again: word for word, “it makes three years”.

**For (up to now).** For something that started in the past and is still going on, Catalan uses the present, not a past: {{Fa tres anys que visc aquí.}} “I've been living here for three years”, word for word “it makes three years that I live here”. Or: {{Visc aquí des de fa tres anys.}} The question is {{Quant de temps fa que…?}} “How long have you been…?”

**Since.** {{des de}} + a moment: {{Treballo aquí des del 2020.}} “I've worked here since 2020.” {{Estic malalt des de dilluns.}} “I've been sick since Monday.” Its partner is {{fins a}} “until”: {{des de les nou fins a les cinc}} “from nine to five”.

table: I've been living here for two years.
{{Visc aquí des de fa dos anys.}}
I've been living here for two years.

blocks.p: **Dates.** A year is said as a number: {{el 2024}} “in 2024”, {{dos mil vint-i-quatre}}. A date: {{el tres de maig}} “(on) May 3”. The months have a small letter: {{gener}}, {{febrer}}, {{març}}, {{abril}}, {{maig}}, {{juny}}, {{juliol}}, {{agost}}, {{setembre}}, {{octubre}}, {{novembre}}, {{desembre}}. Before a vowel, {{de}} becomes {{d'}}: {{el vint d'abril}}, {{el dotze d'octubre}}.

lessons.title: Tell what happened, step by step
lessons.summary: Tell a story in order, from start to finish: “First we had dinner, then we went dancing, and in the end we walked home.”
lessons.topic: The past with {{anar}} + {{primer, després, llavors, al final}}; {{quan}}; weak pronouns before {{vaig}}: {{la vaig veure}}

goal.t: Primer vam sopar, després vam anar a ballar i al final vam tornar a peu.
goal.tr: First we had dinner, then we went dancing, and in the end we walked home.

dialog.t: Què vau fer dissabte?
dialog.tr: What did you guys do on Saturday?

dialog.t: Primer vam sopar en un restaurant del Born.
dialog.tr: First we had dinner at a restaurant in the Born.

dialog.tr: And then?

blocks.p: **Putting events in order.** Each event is a verb in the past with {{anar}} (lesson 24), and little words link them: {{primer}} “first”, {{després}} “then, afterwards”, {{llavors}} “then, at that point”, {{de sobte}} “suddenly”, {{al final}} “in the end”.
**When.** {{quan}} “when” joins two events: {{Quan vam arribar, vam trucar a la Marta.}} “When we arrived, we called Marta.”

**Pronouns in the past.** A weak pronoun goes before the helper {{vaig, vas, va…}}, never between the helper and the verb: {{La vaig veure.}} “I saw her.” {{Ho vaig dir.}} “I said it.” {{Em vaig llevar tard.}} “I got up late.”

ex.t: Primer vam visitar el museu i després vam dinar.
ex.tr: First we visited the museum, and then we had lunch.

ex.t: Quan vaig arribar a casa, em vaig dutxar.
ex.tr: When I got home, I took a shower.

ex.t: De sobte va començar a ploure.
La vaig veure al concert, però ella no em va veure.
ex.tr: I saw her at the concert, but she didn't see me.

ex.t: Al final ho vam deixar per a un altre dia.
ex.tr: In the end we left it for another day.

ex.t: Ens vam conèixer fa deu anys a Londres.
ex.tr: We met ten years ago in London.
ex.note: {{conèixer-se}} “to meet each other”

blocks.tip: To keep a story going, react with {{De debò?}} “Really?”, {{I llavors?}} “And then what?”, or {{No m'ho puc creure!}} “I can't believe it!”.

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: Say what you're in the middle of doing: “I can't talk now, I'm driving.”
lessons.topic: {{estar}} + gerund: {{estic treballant}}; gerunds in {{-ant, -ent, -int}}

goal.t: Ara no puc parlar, estic conduint.
goal.tr: I can't talk now, I'm driving.

dialog.t: Hola, fill! Què fas?
dialog.tr: Hi, son! What are you doing?

dialog.t: Hola, mama. Estic cuinant: tinc convidats.
dialog.tr: Hi, Mom. I'm cooking: I have guests.

dialog.t: Ah, i què estàs fent?
dialog.tr: Oh, and what are you making?

dialog.t: Una truita de patates. Però ara no puc parlar gaire…
dialog.tr: A potato omelet. But I can't really talk right now…

dialog.t: D'acord, fins demà!
dialog.tr: OK, talk to you tomorrow!

blocks.p: **In the middle of it.** {{estar}} (lesson 9) + a gerund says what is going on at this very moment: {{Estic cuinant.}} “I'm cooking (right now).” You need it less often than English “-ing”, because the plain present already means “I'm doing” (lesson 12). Use it to stress that you're in the middle of it.

blocks.means: the “-ing” form of a verb: cooking, reading. In Catalan it ends in {{-ant}}, {{-ent}} or {{-int}}.

blocks.p: **Pronouns.** A weak pronoun goes before {{estar}} or on the end of the gerund, never between them: {{L'estic llegint.}} = {{Estic llegint-lo.}} “I'm reading it.” {{M'estic dutxant.}} = {{Estic dutxant-me.}} “I'm taking a shower.”

ex.t: Ara mateix t'estic escrivint un missatge.
ex.tr: I'm writing you a message right now.

ex.note: these days: still going on

blocks.tip: {{ara mateix}} “right now” and {{en aquest moment}} “at the moment” often go with it. When you're busy: {{Ara no et puc atendre.}} “I can't deal with you right now.”

The gerund of {{fer}} is {{fent}}.
A gerund goes with {{estar}}, never with {{ser}}.

The pronoun goes before {{estar}} or on the end of the gerund, never between them.

lessons.title: Say what things were like and what you used to do
lessons.summary: Describe the past and your habits back then: “When I was little, I lived in a village and walked to school.”
lessons.topic: The imperfect: {{parlava}}, {{vivia}}; {{era}}, {{feia}}, {{tenia}}, {{hi havia}}

goal.t: Quan era petita, vivia en un poble i anava a l'escola a peu.
goal.tr: When I was little, I lived in a village and walked to school.
goal.note: said by a woman; a man says {{petit}}

dialog.t: Àvia, com era el barri quan eres jove?
dialog.tr: Grandma, what was the neighborhood like when you were young?

dialog.t: Era molt diferent! No hi havia tants cotxes i tothom es coneixia.
dialog.tr: It was very different! There weren't so many cars, and everybody knew each other.

dialog.t: I què feies els diumenges?
dialog.tr: And what did you do on Sundays?

dialog.t: Anàvem a missa i després ballàvem sardanes a la plaça.
dialog.tr: We went to Mass, and then we danced sardanes in the square.

dialog.t: I tenies televisió?
dialog.tr: And did you have a TV?

dialog.t: No! Escoltàvem la ràdio.
dialog.tr: No! We listened to the radio.

blocks.means: a past tense for how things were and what used to happen, the background of a story: “it was sunny”, “we used to live there”.

blocks.p: **What it's for.** The imperfect describes the past as it was going on: what things were like ({{Era molt diferent.}} “It was very different.”) and what happened again and again ({{Els diumenges anàvem a la platja.}} “On Sundays we used to go to the beach.”). English often says “used to” or “would”; Catalan simply uses the imperfect.
{{-ar}} verbs take {{-ava}}; all the others take {{-ia}}. “I” and “he, she” are the same, so the context (or a pronoun) makes it clear: {{Jo vivia a Vic i ell vivia a Girona.}}

**A few to learn by heart.** {{ser}}: {{era}}, {{eres}}, {{era}}, {{érem}}, {{éreu}}, {{eren}}. {{fer}}: {{feia}}, {{feies}}, {{feia}}… In the same way {{dir}} gives {{deia}}, {{veure}} {{veia}}, {{beure}} {{bevia}}, {{escriure}} {{escrivia}}. And {{hi ha}} becomes {{hi havia}} “there was, there were”.

ex.t: Quan era petit, jugava a futbol cada dia.
ex.tr: When I was little, I played soccer every day.
We used to live in Sabadell.

ex.t: A l'escola hi havia un professor molt estricte.
ex.tr: At school there was a very strict teacher.

ex.t: Feia molta calor i no tenia aigua.
ex.tr: It was very hot, and I didn't have any water.

ex.t: El meu avi sempre deia que el temps és or.
ex.tr: My grandfather always used to say that time is gold.
What did you want to be when you grew up?
ex.note: {{de gran}} “as a grown-up”

blocks.tip: {{abans}} “before, in the old days” and {{quan era petit}} “when I was little” are the classic ways to start talking about how things were.

mistakes.wrong: Quan vaig ser petit, vaig viure a Vic.
mistakes.right: Quan era petit, vivia a Vic.
mistakes.tr: When I was little, I lived in Vic.
mistakes.why: How things were, over a long time: the imperfect.

mistakes.tr: We used to live in Sabadell.
mistakes.why: Verbs not in {{-ar}} take {{-ia}}, and “we” is {{-íem}}: {{vivíem}}.
Like {{hi ha}}, {{hi havia}} doesn't change for the plural.

practice.tr: When I was little, I lived in Vic.
practice.why: How things were over a long time: the imperfect, {{vivia}}.

lessons.title: Tell a story with its background
lessons.summary: Set the scene, then say what happened: “It was very sunny when we got to the beach.”
lessons.topic: The imperfect for the background, the past with {{anar}} for the events; {{estava}} + gerund; {{mentre}}

goal.t: Feia molt de sol quan vam arribar a la platja.
goal.tr: It was very sunny when we got to the beach.

dialog.t: Què et va passar ahir? Vas arribar tard!
dialog.tr: What happened to you yesterday? You were late!

dialog.t: Uf! Estava esperant l'autobús i va començar a ploure.
dialog.tr: Ugh! I was waiting for the bus, and it started to rain.

dialog.t: I no tenies paraigua?
dialog.tr: And you didn't have an umbrella?

dialog.t: No! I quan va arribar l'autobús, estava ple.
dialog.tr: No! And when the bus came, it was full.

dialog.t: Quina mala sort!
dialog.tr: What bad luck!

dialog.t: Al final vaig agafar un taxi.
dialog.tr: In the end I took a taxi.

blocks.p: **Two pasts, two jobs.** In a story, the imperfect paints the background: the weather, the time, what things were like, what was going on ({{feia sol}}, {{eren les deu}}, {{estava cansat}}). The past with {{anar}} moves the story on: what happened, one event after another ({{vaig arribar}}, {{va començar a ploure}}).

table: {{Eren les dues de la nit…}} It was two in the morning…
{{…i va sonar el telèfon.}} …and the phone rang.
{{Estava molt cansada…}} I was very tired…
{{…i em vaig adormir al sofà.}} …and I fell asleep on the couch.

blocks.p: **Was doing.** {{estava}} + a gerund (lesson 29) is for what was going on when something happened: {{Estava dormint quan va trucar.}} “I was sleeping when he called.” {{mentre}} “while” joins two things going on at the same time: {{Mentre cuinava, escoltava la ràdio.}} “While I was cooking, I was listening to the radio.”
Ask yourself: is it the scene, or the next thing that happened? The scene: the imperfect. The next thing: {{vaig}} + a verb.

ex.t: Plovia quan vaig sortir de casa.
ex.tr: It was raining when I left home.

ex.t: Estàvem sopant quan va arribar en Pere.
ex.tr: We were having dinner when Pere arrived.

ex.t: Era tard i no hi havia ningú al carrer.
ex.tr: It was late, and there was nobody in the street.
While I was working, he was sleeping.

ex.t: Com que tenia gana, vaig comprar un entrepà.
ex.tr: Since I was hungry, I bought a sandwich.
ex.note: {{com que}} “since, as” (lesson 38)

ex.t: La vaig conèixer quan vivia a Londres.
ex.tr: I met her when I was living in London.

blocks.tip: {{Què et va passar?}} “What happened to you?”, {{Quina sort!}} “How lucky!” and {{Quina mala sort!}} “What bad luck!” keep a story going.

mistakes.why: What was going on when something happened: the imperfect, {{estava}}.

mistakes.right: Feia sol i de sobte va començar a ploure.
mistakes.tr: It was sunny, and suddenly it started to rain.
mistakes.why: {{de sobte}} “suddenly” marks an event: the past with {{anar}}.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say what's bigger, cheaper or better, and what's the best of all: “Barcelona is bigger than Girona, but Girona is quieter.”
lessons.topic: {{més… que}}, {{menys… que}}, {{tan… com}}; {{millor}}, {{pitjor}}; {{el més…}}; {{-íssim}}

goal.t: Barcelona és més gran que Girona, però Girona és més tranquil·la.
goal.tr: Barcelona is bigger than Girona, but Girona is quieter.

dialog.t: Quin pis t'agrada més?
dialog.tr: Which apartment do you like better?

dialog.t: El de Gràcia és més bonic, però el de Sants és més barat.
dialog.tr: The one in Gràcia is nicer, but the one in Sants is cheaper.

dialog.t: I quin és més gran?
dialog.tr: And which one is bigger?

dialog.t: Són igual de grans. Però el de Gràcia té més llum.
dialog.tr: They're just as big. But the one in Gràcia gets more light.

dialog.t: Doncs per a mi, el de Gràcia és el millor.
dialog.tr: Then for me, the Gràcia one is the best.

blocks.p: **More and less.** {{més}} + adjective + {{que}} is “-er than, more… than”, and {{menys}} + adjective + {{que}} is “less… than”: {{El metro és més ràpid que l'autobús.}} “The subway is faster than the bus.” {{És menys car que l'altre.}} “It's less expensive than the other one.” Catalan has no “-er” ending: every adjective works with {{més}}.

**As… as.** {{tan}} + adjective + {{com}}: {{La Marta és tan alta com el seu germà.}} “Marta is as tall as her brother.” With a noun it's {{tant… com}}, which agrees: {{No tinc tants amics com tu.}} “I don't have as many friends as you.” And {{igual de}} + adjective is “just as”: {{Són igual de cars.}} “They're just as expensive.”
**Better and worse.** {{bo}} “good” → {{millor}} “better”; {{dolent}} “bad” → {{pitjor}} “worse”. They're the same for women: {{una idea millor}}; plural {{millors}}, {{pitjors}}.

**The most.** Put the article in front: {{el més car}} “the most expensive”, {{la més gran}} “the biggest”, {{el millor}} “the best”. “In” after it is {{de}}: {{el millor restaurant de la ciutat}} “the best restaurant in town”.

**Really, really.** {{-íssim}} on an adjective means “extremely”: {{car}} → {{caríssim}} “super expensive”, {{bo}} → {{boníssim}} “delicious”. It agrees like any adjective: {{caríssima}}, {{caríssims}}.

ex.t: El tren és més ràpid que el cotxe.
ex.tr: The train is faster than the car.

ex.t: Aquest hotel és menys car que l'altre.
ex.tr: This hotel is less expensive than the other one.

ex.t: La meva germana és tan alta com jo.
ex.tr: My sister is as tall as I am.

ex.t: És el millor restaurant de la ciutat.
ex.tr: It's the best restaurant in town.

ex.t: Avui fa més calor que ahir.

blocks.tip: {{tranquil·la}} has Catalan's “flying dot”, {{l·l}}: a long {{l}}, as in {{pel·lícula}} “movie”, {{col·legi}} “school”, {{il·lusió}} “excitement”.

mistakes.why: “Than” is {{que}}.
{{millor}} already means “better”: no {{més}}.

mistakes.tr: She's as tall as I am.
mistakes.why: After {{tan}}, “as” is {{com}}.
